title: Simple integer equations should exist whose lack of solutions is unprovable

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Simple integer equations should exist whose lack of solutions is unprovable

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Although known universal integer equations are very complicated (the simplest having 9 variables and an immense number of terms), there should be much simpler integer equations for which the absence of solutions can never be proved from the standard axioms of arithmetic.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: so that in fact there are in the end rather simple integer equations for which the absence of solutions can never be proved from the normal axioms of arithmetic.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Implications for Mathematics and Its Foundations” (from p. 772), p. 789. Scope: Diophantine equations and Peano arithmetic

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-35: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.62

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The existence claim is mathematically testable after a simplicity criterion is chosen, but public resources do not by themselves supply the required small independent equation. Resolving it likely requires a new construction and proof.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fix Peano arithmetic, a Diophantine syntax, and a simplicity measure, then exhibit a substantially smaller equation and prove both that it has no integer solutions and that Peano arithmetic cannot prove this fact. A proof that no equation below a threshold has the property would refute a quantified version.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
"Much simpler" has no specified metric or threshold.

Known universal constructions may not meet the intended simplicity.

Proving independence and actual absence of solutions simultaneously is difficult.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The existence of some Diophantine equations with unprovable insolubility follows from the DPRM theorem plus incompleteness, and the known universal examples are the complicated ones the text describes. The further claim that rather simple equations of this kind exist is an existence conjecture with no supplied witness. Catalogs of small equations support the contrast in size and do not exhibit an independent simple case.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fix a size measure such as number of variables and total degree, then search for an equation below a stated size whose insolubility is provable in a standard metatheory and unprovable in ordinary arithmetic. Exhibiting one confirms the existence claim at that size; a proof that every equation below the size is decidable in arithmetic would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Known universal equations are large, and proving a specific small equation independent of arithmetic is a separate theorem.

Rather simple needs an explicit size cutoff.

A true Pi-1 statement can be independent, so failure to find a solution below a search bound is inconclusive.
